title.narrative: Output 6.4. Increased capacity of Member States to strengthen legislation, polices and measures to ensure equal opportunities and treatment in the world of work for persons with disabilities and other persons in vulnerable situations

description.narrative: In 2022 the review of the existing national policy on HIV and AIDS and its Implementation Guidelines was undertaken to reflect emerging issues since it was last revised to provide a more comprehensive platform for Strategic responses to this and other infections. The revised policy, which was adopted in December 2022, captures new information on HIV and AIDs epidemic locally and around the world. Within Nigeria, new evidence has emerged from surveys such as the Nigeria National HIV/AIDS Indicator and Impact Survey, routine surveys like the IBBS, ANC, NAHRHS as well as smaller studies like the prison study. Global best practices have also made recommendations on guidelines for prevention, treatment, and care services such as the test and treat strategy, self-testing kits. Therefore, the gaps identified in the National workplace policy on HIV and AIDS were updated also taking cognizance that Occupational safety and health is now a Fundamental principle and right at work .The revised policy will provide an enabling legal and policy framework for coordinated response amongst world of work actors. It would also form the basis for HIV workplace programmes aimed at ensuring universal access to prevention, treatment, care and support for all Nigerians in line with efforts to mitigate the impact of the HIV epidemic in Nigeria. In collaboration with Ministries of Labour and Employers' and Workers' Organizations, the development and implementation of national and enterprise level workplace policies were carried out in pursuance of the Decent Work Agenda and as part of National HIV and AIDS Strategies. It would also foster ILO collaboration with partners in high burden states to implement innovative HIV workplace interventions in the public and private sectors as well as the formal and informal economies. The ILO Code of Practice on HIV/AIDS and the ILO Recommendation provide the framework for ILO’s support to member States. In 2022, ILO provided normative support to its constituents to review the National HIV workplace policy and its Implementation guideline. ILO coordinated the establishment of strategic partnerships in November 2022 to facilitate the successful review by securing the buy in of key stakeholders. To ensure buy in of partners, ILO also facilitated and undertook planning meetings with various partners including ILO constituents, National Agency for the control of AIDs, Civil society organizations, Health Management Organizations affiliated to the National Health Insurance Schemes, service providers and networks of people living with HIV/AIDs (NEPWHAN). Throughout the process ILO provided technical oversight and organized National consultative workshops as well as the validation of the policy and its implementation guideline. ILO supported the technical drafting developed the concept note and budgets and undertook planning and preparatory meetings with National and State level stakeholders. ILO also delivered technical presentations on ILO standards concerning HIV and AIDs. The ILO also provided resource persons for the National consultation and validation. The validation workshop was held in November 2022 in Abuja.

Output 6.3. Increased capacity of Member States to develop gender-responsive legislation, policies and measures for a world of work free from violence and harassment

description.narrative: To ensure the application in practice of Convention No. 190, the National Union of Textile and Garment Workers and the National Association of Textile and Garment Employers reviewed their existing collective bargaining agreements and agreed to include new provisions on preventing and eliminating violence and harassment at work, in line with relevant standards. In particular, the new text of the collective agreement foresees that policy measures are put in place to prevent and address violence and harassment in the world of work and recognize the right of textile workers to a world of work free from violence and harassment, including gender-based violence and harassment. It also seeks to eliminate inequalities that perpetuate discrimination, violence, and harassment in the world of work including for workers living with HIV and disabilities. The text of the new collective bargaining agreement was adopted in July 2023. In collaboration with ACTRAV and with support from the ILO HIV Project, ILO in 2022 provided normative guidance on the provisions of ILO Convention 190 on violence and Harassment with a view to revising the existing collective bargaining agreement in the textile sector between the National Union of Textile and Garment Workers and National Association of Textile and Garment Employers. Through a capacity building workshop, ILO strengthened the capacity of the textile sector trade unions and employers to develop policies and programs to address and prevent Gender Based violence and harassment as occupational health and safety workplace issue and ensure gender equality and equal treatment for men, women, PLHIV and other groups in vulnerable situations. Following this initiative, ILO engaged a consultant to undertake a gap analysis of the existing collecting bargaining agreements of the Textile sector taking into account provisions of the ILO Convention 190. ILO also facilitated and undertook planning and preparatory meetings with the stakeholder’s various partners including National Joint Industrial Negotiating Council composed of members from the National Union of Textile and Garment Workers and National Association of Textile and Garment Employers. ILO provided technical guidance in the development of the concept note, terms of reference and review of various draft reports from the consultants. ILO also delivered technical presentations on ILO Convention 190 on violence and Harassment and its interlinkages to HIV. 33 participants were trained (21 men and 10 women) targeted at the National Joint Industrial Negotiating Council who are vested with the power of formal negotiation relating to industrial relations matters in the textile sector. Participants were educated on GBVH as an occupational health and safety workplace issue and provided the guiding framework for developing workplace policies to prevent and address GBVH at the workplace.
